summary: Lists requirements and desired properties of NEMO route optimization for aeronautics and space exploration networks. It draws on input from aeronautical communications experts outside the IETF.

eli5.summary: Airplanes and spacecraft carry whole networks as they travel. This note lists what such moving networks need so their messages can take good paths.

questions: what are nemo route optimization requirements for aeronautics
mobile networks in space and aircraft
why is nemo not suitable without route optimization
subtitle: What aircraft and spacecraft networks need for efficient routing when mobile.

tldr.problem: Aircraft and spacecraft carry entire networks that move globally, but the standard NEMO (Network Mobility) protocol routes all traffic through a distant home agent, adding unacceptable delay and overhead.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists nine required characteristics and five desirable properties that a NEMO route optimization solution must support, including multihoming, low latency, high availability, scalable signaling, and strong security for safety-critical systems.
tldr.outcome: NEMO became viable for real operational use in aeronautics and space only when these route optimization requirements could be met.

today: RFC 5522 remains the definitive specification of requirements for NEMO route optimization in aeronautics and space exploration. As ICAO develops IP-based air traffic systems and NASA plans spacecraft networking, these requirements continue to guide protocol design.

sections.title: Network Mobility in Aerospace
sections.content:
Aircraft and spacecraft each carry an entire network of computing devices, sensors, and avionics equipment. As they move, they use NEMO (Network Mobility), an extension of Mobile IPv6, to keep their IP addresses constant even as their connection points change.

However, standard NEMO routes all traffic through a home agent—a fixed server that tracks the moving network's location. For an aircraft flying across continents, this creates a problem: data destined for the aircraft must travel all the way back to the home agent's location before being routed to the plane's current position. This adds enormous delays and link overhead that are unacceptable in safety-critical systems.
sections.eli5: Imagine asking a question by sending a letter to your home address, and your parents forwarding it to wherever you are now. That takes forever. Better to just send it directly to where you are.

sections.title: Three Operational Domains
sections.content:
The RFC describes three separate domains of aviation communications, each with different requirements:

Air Traffic Services (ATS) handles safety-critical navigation and control, similar to an air traffic control system. Airline Operational Services (AOS) carries flight management and business data like fuel status and passenger manifests. Passenger Information and Entertainment Services (PIES) provides Internet access to passengers.

Each domain faces different performance and security requirements. For spacecraft, the RFC covers both unmanned vehicles that send telemetry and commands, and manned missions where astronauts may use personal networks. Space communications add further challenges like asymmetric bandwidth (fast downloads, slow uploads) and extreme propagation delays for deep space.
sections.eli5: Planes carry three types of networks: critical systems for flying the plane, business systems for running the airline, and passenger Wi-Fi. Each needs different treatment.

sections.title: Nine Required Characteristics
sections.content:
The document defines nine absolute requirements:

Separability: Some flows should bypass optimization and use the home agent tunnel for recording or security. Multihoming: An aircraft may use multiple access links simultaneously (VDL, satellite, HF radio) and need independent route optimization per link. Latency: Optimization must not block packets during setup; they must fall back to the home agent tunnel. Availability: No single point of failure; the solution must work with redundant routers and home agents.

Packet Loss: The scheme must not introduce additional packet loss or duplication. Scalability: It must serve hundreds of thousands of aircraft without overloading ground networks or the global routing system. Efficient Signaling: Signaling overhead must be minimal since aeronautical links are expensive and limited. Security: For ATS and AOS, the solution must prevent exposure of the mobile network prefix, validate address ownership, and ensure only authorized routers can update bindings. Adaptability: New transport protocols and security mechanisms must remain usable.
sections.eli5: A solution has to split traffic when needed, use multiple connections, work fast, survive failures, not lose data, handle thousands of planes, use small messages, stay secure, and let new applications work.

sections.title: Five Desirable Properties
sections.content:
Beyond the requirements, the document lists properties that would help deployment:

Configuration: Simple setup and automatic failover reduce human error and operational risk. Nesting: Supporting nested mobile routers (for personal networks within the main aircraft network) would enable some scenarios, though it is not immediately needed. System Impact: Lower complexity in the overall network architecture makes the system easier to deploy and maintain. VMN Support: Supporting Visiting Mobile Nodes (personal devices like laptops that passengers bring aboard) would enhance the PIES domain. Generality: A solution that works beyond aviation—in vehicular networks or consumer electronics—would benefit from wider research and vendor support.
sections.eli5: Nice to have: simple setup, support for networks inside networks, not too complicated, passenger devices work, and it works in cars and trucks too.

sections.title: Why This Matters for Aerospace
sections.content:
Aeronautical and space networks face challenges that amplify the problems with NEMO's home agent tunneling:

Long routes and propagation delays: Aircraft cross multiple continents, and data links like VDL mode 2 run at only 8 kbps with high queueing delays. Satellite links add seconds of propagation delay. Forcing all traffic through a distant home agent is unacceptable. Constrained bandwidth: Every byte of protocol overhead displaces useful data. Space communications have even tighter bandwidth constraints. Fragmentation risk: Error-prone air-ground links mean fragmented packets are at higher risk of loss. Single points of failure: For command-and-control and safety-of-life systems, losing the home agent disrupts all communications.

Without route optimization, NEMO was considered too risky for operational deployment in these sectors. The requirements in this document were necessary to make NEMO a viable option.
sections.eli5: Planes are far from home, messages are slow and costly, and a broken link back to headquarters is dangerous. So we need a way to route messages straight to the plane.
